title: BlockSpec index_map returns the wrong rank
error: Index map function index_map at scripts/gen_mistakes.py:28 for x_ref must return 2 values to match block_shape=(2, 128). Currently returning 1 values.
why: index_map runs once per grid step and it has to hand back one coordinate for every axis of the block shape you declared. A (2, 128) block is two-dimensional, so index_map needs to return a two-element tuple, but this one returns just `(i,)`. The error spells out the mismatch directly: it wants 2 values and gets 1. Whenever you see that pattern, count the axes in your block_shape and check the length of the tuple your index_map returns against it, they need to match even when one axis never moves.

title: out_shape disagrees with what the kernel writes
error: Invalid shape for `swap`. Ref shape: (8, 128). Expected shape: (8, 128). Value shape: (8, 256). Transforms: (NDIndexer(indices=(Slice(start=0, size=8, stride=1), Slice(start=0, size=128, stride=1)), shape=(8, 128), int_indexer_shape=(), validate=False),).
why: out_shape isn't a description of what the kernel reads, it's the caller's promise about the physical buffer the kernel writes into. Pallas allocates the output ref from that shape and then checks every write against it, so when the kernel concatenates two (8, 128) blocks into a (8, 256) value and tries to store it in a ref sized (8, 128), the write fails. The error names both shapes side by side, ref shape and value shape, which is the fastest way to spot this class of bug. The fix is to size out_shape from what the kernel actually produces, not from the shape of its inputs.

title: fori_loop carry structure mismatch
error:
scan body function carry input and carry output must have the same pytree structure, but they differ:

The input carry component loop_carry[1] is a tuple of length 2 but the corresponding component of the carry output is a tuple of length 3, so the lengths do not match.

Revise the function so that the carry output has the same pytree structure as the carry input.
why: jax.lax.fori_loop traces the loop body once and reuses that trace for every iteration, so the carry it returns has to match the structure of the carry it received, same number of elements, same types, every time through. This body takes a two-element tuple in and returns a three-element tuple, adding an extra value to what it hands back. The error names the exact mismatch, input carry has length 2 and output carry has length 3, which is enough on its own to tell you where to look. Whatever a loop body accepts as carry, it must return in that same shape, nothing added and nothing dropped.

title: reading a ref with wrong-rank indexing
error: `indices` must not be longer than `shape`: indices=(slice(None, None, None), slice(None, None, None), 0), shape=(8, 128)
why: A ref only accepts as many indices as it has dimensions, and that dimension count comes from the block shape declared in the BlockSpec, not from the original array before blocking. Here x_ref is a 2D block, so indexing it with three entries, `x_ref[:, :, 0]`, asks for an axis that doesn't exist. The error reports this literally: indices must not be longer than shape, and then prints both lengths so you can compare them. When you write a ref index, count against the block's own rank, since that's the shape the kernel actually sees.

title: index_map written for the wrong grid rank
why: Pallas calls index_map once per grid step and passes it one positional argument per grid dimension, so a 1D grid, declared as grid=(2,), only ever supplies one argument. This index_map is written for two grid axes, `index_map(i, j)`, but only `i` ever arrives. The error is plain Python surfacing through Pallas: missing 1 required positional argument, 'j', which is the same message you'd get calling any function with too few arguments. Match the parameter count of index_map to the number of entries in your grid tuple, not to the rank of the array you're blocking.

title: dtype mismatch on accumulation
error: Invalid dtype for `swap`. Ref dtype: float32. Value dtype: bfloat16.
why: Writing into a ref checks dtype as strictly as it checks shape, and ordinary arithmetic in JAX doesn't upcast a low-precision value just because you added a Python float to it. x_ref holds bfloat16, and `x_ref[...] + 1.0` stays bfloat16 under JAX's weak-type promotion rules, so storing that straight into an f32 output ref fails at the write. The error states both dtypes outright, ref dtype float32 against value dtype bfloat16, which tells you the fix without needing to read further into the trace. Before a store, cast explicitly to the ref's declared dtype with .astype rather than counting on the arithmetic to do it for you.

title: The block that cannot fit: VMEM overflow at compile time
error:
RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: XLA:TPU compile permanent error. Ran out of memory in memory space vmem. Used 128.00M of 127.94M vmem. Exceeded vmem capacity by 64.0K.

Program vmem requirement 128.00M:
 scoped 128.00M

 Largest program allocations in vmem:

 1. Size: 64.00M
    Operator: op_name="jit(wrapped)/pallas_call"
    Shape: u8[67108864]{0}
    Unpadded size: 64.00M
    Tag: input window allocation for operator input 0. The window shape is f32[4096,4096], while the full shape is f32[4096,4096]. This allocation is single buffered.

 2. Size: 64.00M
    Operator: op_name="jit(wrapped)/pallas_call"
    Tag: output window allocation for operator output 0. The window shape is f32[4096,4096], while the full shape is f32[4096,4096].
why: Captured on a real v6e-1 (jax 0.11): a single 4096x4096 f32 block is 64 MB, the output window is another 64 MB, and the chip has 127.94 MB of VMEM, so the compile fails by exactly 64 KB. Read the error the way the compiler wrote it: those "window allocation" lines are your BlockSpecs made physical, one allocation per ref, and "single buffered" tells you pipelining could not even double-buffer. The schedule, not the algorithm, is what did not fit; carve the array into grid steps and the same elementwise body compiles untouched.

title: The (8, 128) lattice, enforced by the lowering
error:
The Pallas TPU lowering currently requires that the last two dimensions of your block shape are divisible by 8 and 128 respectively, or be equal to the respective dimensions of the overall array. Block spec for args[0] in pallas_call <lambda> at labs/measurement-day.ipynb has block shape (Blocked(block_size=7), Blocked(block_size=100)), array shape (70, 300), and index_map { lambda ; a:i32[] b:i32[]. let in (a, b) }, in memory space <MemorySpace.DEFAULT: 'default'>.
See details at https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/pallas/grid_blockspec.html#pallas-blockspec
why: Captured on a real v6e-1 (jax 0.11): the vector registers are (8, 128) tiles, so the lowering demands block shapes whose last two dimensions are multiples of 8 and 128 (or the whole array). This is chapter 07's vocabulary surfacing as an error: the message even prints the index_map back at you as a jaxpr. A (7, 100) block cannot be laid onto the lattice; pick block shapes on the lattice and let the edge padding come from the array shape instead.
